title: Adding & Subtracting Decimals
subtitle: One rule, and one mistake almost everybody makes.
objectives: Identify the place value of each digit after a decimal point
Add and subtract decimals by aligning the decimal points
Use zeros to fill empty place values
Estimate an answer to check whether a result is sensible
Solve word problems involving money and measurement

cards.title: A race is won by two hundredths of a second
cards.text: Lap times look like 1:23.456. Those digits after the point are the whole sport. Get them wrong and you're not close — you're nowhere.

cards.title: Each place is ten times smaller
cards.text: Going right from the decimal point, every column is worth a tenth of the one before it.
points: **First place = tenths.** 0.4 is four tenths.
**Second place = hundredths.** 0.04 is four hundredths.
**Third place = thousandths.** 0.004.
**0.4 is ten times bigger than 0.04.** Same digit, different worth.

cards.title: Split times are decimal subtraction
cards.text: That −0.284 flashing on screen is your time minus the record. The game is doing this lesson every lap.
points: **The delta is a subtraction**, done to the thousandth.
**Round it to 1:23 and the delta vanishes.** Precision is the point.

question.explain: 0.7 — that's seven tenths, which is 0.70. More digits doesn't mean a bigger number. Compare place by place, starting at the left.

cards.title: Line up the decimal points
cards.text: That's it. That's the whole method for adding and subtracting decimals. Everything else you already know from whole numbers.
points: **Stack the numbers with the points in one column.**
**Fill any gaps with zeros.**
**Bring the point straight down** into the answer.
**Then add or subtract exactly as normal.**

cards.title: The mistake, and the fix
cards.text: Tap between the two. Lining up the right-hand edge is what most people do wrong, and you can see why it breaks.

question.explain: 16.25. Write 12.5 as 12.50 first so both have two decimal places, then add straight down.

cards.title: Adding zeros changes nothing
cards.text: 12.5 and 12.50 and 12.500 are the same number. Zeros on the end of a decimal are free.
points: **Use them to make both numbers the same length.**
**It makes the columns line up** without you having to think.
**Careful:** 12.05 is not 12.5. A zero in the middle changes everything.

cards.title: Minecraft coordinates work the same way
cards.text: Your position reads something like X: 128.50, Y: 64.00, Z: −310.25. Those are decimals, and moving is adding to them.
points: **Y: 64.00 is exactly sea level.** The zeros are placeholders.
**Distance travelled** is one coordinate minus another.
**Negative coordinates** work the same — the point stays put.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: You've got the rule. Part 2 is subtraction, checking your work, and money. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Same rule, one extra danger
cards.text: Subtraction uses the identical method. The only new problem is borrowing across a gap you forgot to fill.

cards.title: Fill the gaps before you start
cards.text: For 8.4 − 2.65, write the 8.4 as 8.40 first. Now there's something in the hundredths column to borrow from.
points: **Without the zero** you have nothing to take 5 from.
**The answer is 5.75.**

question.explain: 5.75. Writing 8.4 as 8.40 first gives you a hundredths digit to borrow from.

cards.title: Estimate first, then check
cards.text: Round both numbers to whole numbers and add them in your head. Your real answer should land near that.
points: **You got 16.25.** Close to 17, so it's sensible.
**If you'd got 162.5**, the estimate would have caught it.

cards.title: Making weight is decimal subtraction
cards.text: A weight limit is exact. 62.5 kg means 62.5, and 62.6 means you don't fight.
points: **Weigh 64.3 kg with a 62.5 limit?** You need to lose 1.8 kg.
**That's a subtraction** you'd better get right.
**Rounding to whole kilos** would hide the whole problem.

cards.title: Every price you've ever seen is this
cards.text: Money is decimals with exactly two places. Pesos before the point, centavos after.
points: **₱125.50 + ₱48.75** — same rule, line up the points.
**Always write two decimal places** for money. ₱7.5 should be ₱7.50.
**Change from a note** is a subtraction.

question.text: You pay ₱200 for something costing ₱147.25. How much change? Digits only.
question.explain: ₱52.75. Write ₱200 as 200.00 first, then subtract. The zeros give you something to borrow from.

cards.title: The three mistakes to avoid
cards.text: Almost every wrong answer in this topic is one of these three.
points: **Lining up the right edge** instead of the decimal point.
**Forgetting to fill gaps with zeros** before subtracting.
**Losing the point in the answer.** Bring it straight down.

question.text: Put the method for adding decimals in order.
items: Stack the numbers with the decimal points in line
Fill any empty places with zeros
Bring the decimal point straight down
question.explain: Align, fill, add, bring the point down. Do it in that order and the arithmetic takes care of itself.

terms.def: The dot separating whole numbers from parts of a whole.
The first place after the point. 0.4 is four tenths.
The second place after the point. 0.04.
The third place after the point. 0.004.
What a digit is worth because of where it sits.
A rough answer used to check a real one is sensible.
Borrowing from the column to the left when subtracting.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Line up the decimal points.** That's the whole rule.
**Fill gaps with zeros.** 8.4 becomes 8.40.
**Bring the point straight down** into the answer.
**Estimate first** so a wrong answer can't slip past you.

quiz.text: In the number 45.376, what is the digit 7 worth?
quiz.explain: Seven hundredths. Counting right from the point: 3 is tenths, 7 is hundredths, 6 is thousandths.
quiz.objective: Identify the place value of each digit after a decimal point

quiz.explain: 20.45. Write 15.6 as 15.60 first, then add straight down with the points in line.
quiz.objective: Add and subtract decimals by aligning the decimal points

quiz.explain: 5.73. Write 9.2 as 9.20 so there's a hundredths digit to borrow from.
quiz.objective: Use zeros to fill empty place values

quiz.explain: 0.8. Compare from the left: 8 tenths beats 7, 1 and 6 tenths. More digits does not mean a bigger number.
quiz.objective: Identify the place value of each digit after a decimal point

quiz.explain: True. A zero on the end of a decimal adds nothing. But 12.05 is different — a zero in the middle changes the place values.
quiz.objective: Use zeros to fill empty place values

quiz.text: What is the most common mistake when adding decimals?
options: Lining the numbers up on the right edge instead of the decimal point
quiz.explain: Right-aligning changes what every digit is worth. Line up the points, not the edges.
quiz.objective: Add and subtract decimals by aligning the decimal points

quiz.text: A 1:24 model of a V8 engine costs ₱237.60. You pay ₱500. What change? Digits only.
quiz.explain: ₱262.40. Write ₱500 as 500.00 first so the columns line up and you have digits to borrow from.
quiz.objective: Solve word problems involving money and measurement

quiz.text: A lap takes 1:23.456. The record is 1:23.740. By how much did you beat it?
quiz.explain: 0.284 seconds. 23.740 − 23.456 = 0.284. That's exactly what a split time on screen is showing you.
quiz.objective: Solve word problems involving money and measurement

quiz.text: Put the steps for adding decimals in the right order.
items: Stack the numbers with the decimal points in line
Fill any empty places with zeros
Bring the decimal point straight down
quiz.explain: Align, fill, add, bring down. In that order the arithmetic is just whole-number addition.
quiz.objective: Add and subtract decimals by aligning the decimal points

quiz.text: You calculate 24.6 + 7.8 and get 103.4. What does estimating tell you?
options: It's right — the numbers are large
It's wrong — it should be about 300
quiz.explain: Rounding gives about 33, and the real answer is 32.4. An answer of 103.4 means the columns weren't aligned.
quiz.objective: Estimate an answer to check whether a result is sensible

quiz.text: A fighter weighs 64.3 kg. The limit is 62.5 kg. How much must they lose? Digits only.
quiz.explain: 1.8 kg. Rounding to whole kilos would have hidden the problem entirely — this is why precision matters.
quiz.objective: Solve word problems involving money and measurement

quiz.text: When subtracting 7.5 − 2.38, you should first write 7.5 as 7.50.
quiz.explain: True. Without the zero there's no hundredths digit to take the 8 from. The answer is 5.12.
quiz.objective: Use zeros to fill empty place values

teacher.summary: Week 3 Maths covers addition and subtraction of decimals, matching the Term 1 weekly scope. The lesson is deliberately built around one rule and one error: align the decimal points, and the mistake is aligning the right-hand edge instead. The interactive figure shows both stackings side by side with both answers, so the error is visible rather than merely described. Week 4 continues the same topic, so this can be taught and then practised.
discussion: Ask which is bigger, 0.7 or 0.65, and why. If he says 0.7 is 0.70, he has place value rather than a rule about counting digits.
Ask him to explain why we add zeros before subtracting. The answer — so there is something to borrow from — shows he understands regrouping.
Ask him to estimate before every answer for a week. It is the single habit that catches misaligned columns.
Ask where he already sees decimals outside maths class. Lap times, prices and weights all count, and noticing them is the point.
teacher.extension: Give him a receipt or a set of lap times and ask for the total and the differences. Real data has awkward numbers of decimal places, which is exactly where the zero-filling habit gets tested.
misconceptions: 'More digits means a bigger number.' 0.109 has more digits than 0.8 but is far smaller. Compare place by place from the left.
'Line up the last digits.' This is the central error of the topic. Align the decimal points; the edges are irrelevant.
'Adding a zero changes the number.' Zeros on the end of a decimal change nothing. Zeros in the middle change everything.
'The decimal point moves during addition.' It stays in its column and comes straight down into the answer.
